summary: This experimental RFC defines an NTP extension field holding a 2-octet checksum complement. Some hardware stamps the exact send time into an outgoing NTP packet, which forces the UDP checksum to change. With the complement in the last bytes of the packet, the hardware can fix things up there instead of rewriting the UDP checksum. It stays interoperable with existing NTP implementations.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7821 defines an extension for the Network Time Protocol (NTP), which hardware can use when it changes a packet's timestamp as it is sent. A value at the end keeps the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) checksum valid without changing its field.

subtitle: An NTP extension lets timestamping hardware correct a packet checksum at its end.

tldr.problem: Hardware may replace an NTP packet's transmit timestamp while sending it, changing the UDP checksum that covers the packet.
tldr.mechanism: A 28-octet NTP extension ends with a 2-octet Checksum Complement, which can cancel the checksum change without rewriting the UDP header.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7821 is Experimental and intended for unauthenticated NTP packets; the supplied metadata says RFC 9748 updates it.

today: RFC 7821 is an Experimental RFC published in March 2016 and has been updated by RFC 9748.

sections.title: Timestamp Changes and UDP Checksums
sections.content:
Some NTP implementations use a hardware timestamping engine to place the accurate transmission time in an outgoing packet. Because NTP travels over UDP, changing the packet payload also changes the value needed in the UDP checksum.

The RFC explains that a device processing the packet in serial order may find it simpler to adjust a field at the end than to return to the UDP header. Its extension provides that later field.
sections.plainLanguage: When timestamping hardware changes an NTP packet, the UDP checksum must still match the packet. RFC 7821 gives the hardware a field at the end to adjust.

sections.title: The Checksum Complement Extension
sections.content:
The Checksum Complement is the final 2 octets of a 28-octet NTP extension field. The other 22 octets are marked MBZ, meaning they must be zero and the receiver must ignore them.

If an NTP packet has other extension fields, this extension must be last. IANA assigned the field type value 0x2005.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is always 28 octets long and ends with a 2-octet complement. Its 22 padding octets must be zero and are ignored by the receiver.

sections.title: Updating the Complement
sections.content:
The sender can include the extension with a zero complement. When the timestamp changes, the timestamping engine writes a complement that cancels the change's effect on the UDP checksum, leaving the checksum field itself unchanged.

The receiver performs its ordinary UDP checksum calculation; it does not need to process the complement specially. A transmitter MAY include the field, and the receiving NTP layer SHOULD ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamping engine changes the complement when it changes the timestamp. The UDP checksum then remains valid, and the receiver checks it as usual.

sections.title: Interoperability with Existing NTP Hosts
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new receiving requirements beyond those in RFC 7822. A host that ignores unknown extension fields can receive packets containing the Checksum Complement.

A host that discards packets with unknown fields cannot interoperate with a sender using this extension. When only one host uses hardware timestamping, the extension should be used only if its peer is known to accept it.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver that ignores unknown NTP extensions can accept this field. A receiver that rejects unknown fields cannot, so the sender must know what its peer supports.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
The Checksum Complement MUST NOT be used when NTP authentication is enabled. Changing the complement would require recalculating the message authentication code, creating a dependency between the two values; the UDP checksum must instead be updated directly.

The extension is intended for use inside an NTP client or server, not by switches or routers between them. The RFC says an intermediate change to NTP content should be treated as a possible man-in-the-middle attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not use the complement with NTP authentication. The RFC intends the field for a client's or server's own timestamping hardware, not for network devices in between.
